extracted.intended_audience: Trainees and researchers preparing NIH R01 and NRSA (F-series) grant applications (graduate students, postdocs, junior faculty) working with institutional grants administrators
extracted.subtask_short: NIH R01 and NRSA grant writing
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, step-by-step guidance for preparing NIH R01 and F-series (NRSA) grant applications, including required sections, formatting, institutional procedures, review process, and scoring criteria. Intended as a workshop handout to guide proposal drafting and review-readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional coordination and Commons ID
rubrics_metrics.description: You will require a Commons ID for submission and will interact with your institution's grants administration office to complete administrative forms and submission steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with your institutional grants administrator to acquire a Commons ID, identify the relevant program announcement, and get help completing the electronic SF424 (R&R) forms. A grants office representative can describe services they provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission formats and Adobe/PDF requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are submitted electronically by uploading Adobe-format documents (PDFs); you must use the proper Adobe version (presently versions 9-11) and follow the 424 instruction package.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare scientific documents as Word files, convert to PDF using the required Adobe version, and upload them into the electronic submission package. Read the 424 instruction package carefully for formatting and technical instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative forms vs scientific documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of information are required: (1) administrative information typed into electronic forms in the submission package, and (2) scientific information prepared as Word documents and uploaded as PDFs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete administrative forms in collaboration with institutional grant administrators. Prepare the scientific narrative (abstract, aims, research strategy, etc.) as Word files and convert to PDF for upload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate Funding Opportunity Announcement (FOA) on grants.gov
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the FOA (e.g., PA-16-309 for NRSA, PA-16-160 for R01) via grants.gov search and download the application package and instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go to grants.gov, use the basic search for the program announcement number, open the opportunity title, and download the 'application package' and instructions (PDF/Word). Read them thoroughly and consult your grants administrator for clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know common FOA codes for NIH mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of parent FOAs for common training and research mechanisms (F30, F31, F32, F33, R01, R21) and their parent announcement numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: F30 - PA-16-306; F31 - parent PA-16-309; F32 - parent PA16-307; F33 - PA-16-310; Parent R01 - PA-16-160; Parent R21 - PA-16-161. Use the correct FOA when preparing and submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recommended grant-writing workbooks and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use established grant-writing workbooks (e.g., The Grant Application Writer’s Workbook) and the chapter references in that workbook to guide preparation of each section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The workbook is recommended (available from grantcentral.com). Much of the training materials are keyed to workbook chapters; consult the workbook chapters referenced throughout this handout for details (e.g., Chapter 7 for Specific Aims, Chapter 9 for Significance, Chapter 15 for Facilities/Equipment, Chapter 18 for Title tips, Chapter 19 for Abstract).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research Plan template and page limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the Research Plan with: Abstract (½ page, 30 lines), Specific Aims (1 page), and Research Strategy (6 or 12 pages) divided into Significance, Innovation (not required for NRSA), and Approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research Strategy total length depends on FOA (6 or 12 pages). Significance typically ½–1 page, Innovation about ½–1 page (if applicable), and Approach uses the remaining pages. Follow the template and FOA-specific page limits exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim-level content (per Aim) for Research Strategy / Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Aim should include: statement of hypothesis; rationale supporting the hypothesis; literature; preliminary data and feasibility; experimental design; expected outcomes and statistical analysis; pitfalls and alternative plans; and timetable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay out Aim I, Aim II, etc., with the above components. Explicitly state hypotheses and rationale, show preliminary data/feasibility, describe experimental design and planned analyses, and anticipate pitfalls with alternative strategies and a timetable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal title guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Title should be compelling, informative, relatively short, descriptive, jargon-free, flexible to encompass future related experiments, and emphasize the payoff of your research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive jargon; make the title general enough to include experiments that may accrue from your results; emphasize research payoff. See workbook Chapter 18 for tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project Summary/Abstract requirements and goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Project Summary/Abstract must be less than 30 lines with ½-inch margins and is the most important part of the proposal — the only part everyone will read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be succinct and pithy; convey all that is in the Specific Aims but in less space. Use critical colleagues to re-review multiple times; choose careful, invested reviewers. It must pass the 'grandma' test: clear, compelling, and understandable rather than technically over-detailed. See workbook Chapter 19.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative (lay description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a short PDF (no more than three or four sentences) as a lay description of your proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This must be clear and impactful and pass the 'grandma' test. Keep it very brief and understandable to a general audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature Cited practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the literature cited in the body of your proposal; compile as part of writing background/significance/rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reference-management software (e.g., Endnote) to build citations while writing. Choose the NIH grant citation style provided with such packages. If space permits, include citations in the text rather than only numbered references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilities and Other Resources description
rubrics_metrics.description: List laboratory facilities, animal science resources, computer, office, and clinical facilities, including the laboratory environment of your advisor/mentor/collaborator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow examples in workbook Chapter 15. Describe what institutional resources will support the proposed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equipment listing
rubrics_metrics.description: List equipment that will be available to perform the proposed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow suggestions in workbook Chapter 15 for completing this section; be specific about major, relevant pieces of equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: CV and Personal Statement content and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: CV should contain academic history, educational background, honors, special achievements, academic record, and publications; personal statement must say why you are the best person to do the proposed work and justify your training/experience and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisors/collaborators must also provide their CVs and personal statements. These are completed on standard forms in the submission package as Word files and uploaded as PDFs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biosketch new-format guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Biosketches allow up to five pages and permit describing up to five of the most significant contributions to science with historical background and up to four relevant products per contribution; a link to a full publication list (e.g., MyBibliography) may be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe central findings and the influence of prior work, and for team science describe your specific role(s). Include relevant non-publication research products (patents, datasets, software, etc.) as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research Support listing (for K awards)
rubrics_metrics.description: For K applications, a faculty advisor must provide research support information listing grants that will sustain the research project during the trainee’s tenure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document that available support is sufficient to sustain the trainee’s research during the award period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Aims structure and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific Aims should have an introductory paragraph (opening sentence, current knowledge, gap in knowledge/unmet need), focus on goals (long-term goal, objective of application, central hypothesis and rationale), and explicit specific aims paragraphs outlining hypothesis, methods, experiments, and expected results with a payoff statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a bullet outline to structure the Specific Aims. End with a payoff statement describing how the world will benefit from your work. Refer to workbook Chapter 7 and sample applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance section content and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance should be approximately ½–1 page and explain the positive effect successful completion will have, including a critical review of the literature, a statement of significance, and discussion of benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly describe the unmet need and how achieving the aims will advance the field; be concise and focused (no more than ~½–1 page). See workbook Chapter 9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation: definition and how to present it
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation is a new and substantially different way of considering/addressing something that results in positive change; document the norm and show how your approach departs from the status quo and projects fundamental progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate Significance vs Innovation. Explain what is standard (methods, interpretations, mechanisms) with citations and then show how your approach departs (paradigm shift vs incremental change). Innovation is not required for NRSA applications; if present, it may be placed in Significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach section structure and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: For each Aim, present hypothesis and rationale; relevant literature and impact; preliminary data and feasibility; detailed experimental design; expected outcomes and statistical analysis; anticipated pitfalls and alternative plans; and a timetable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about methods, analyses, and contingency plans. Demonstrate feasibility with preliminary data and provide realistic timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertebrate Animals section requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the 424 instruction package: state species, strains, ages, sex, and numbers by specific aim; justify the need for live animals; describe procedures to limit discomfort, pain, and distress; and describe euthanasia methods if not consistent with AVMA guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit numeration and justification for animal use per aim, methods to minimize suffering, and details on euthanasia where required. Follow the 424 instruction package exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overview of peer-review process and assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals are submitted to CSR, assigned to a study section, and assigned up to three reviewers who provide preliminary written critiques and an overall score before the meeting; study section discussion selects which proposals are discussed (upper ~50%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand reviewers submit preliminary impact/priority scores to CSR to help triage discussed applications. Each assigned reviewer provides a written critique and preliminary score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nine-point overall scoring system (impact/priority score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scoring uses integers 1–9 where 1 = exceptional and 9 = poor; reviewers provide preliminary impact/priority scores and at the meeting each member votes an integer; the overall score is the average of individual scores multiplied by 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only integers are used for scoring. Preliminary impact scores help determine which applications are discussed. The final overall impact score = (average of integer scores) × 10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five core review criteria (Significance, Investigator, Innovation, Approach, Environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review scores are based on five general criteria: Significance; Investigator; Innovation; Approach; and Environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers evaluate strengths and weaknesses for each criterion and use them to assign the overall impact score. Understand how each criterion maps to descriptors (see individual criterion descriptors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance scoring descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptors map 1–9 to narrative judgments about the likely contribution of achieving the aims to the research field, from 'Achieving the proposed aims is likely to advance the research field in profound and lasting ways' (1) to 'Achieving the proposed aims is unlikely to contribute in any way' (9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these descriptors to anticipate how reviewers will judge the field-advancing potential of your aims. Tailor Significance text to demonstrate likely impact consistent with high-descriptor language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator scoring descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptors evaluate the qualifications of investigators, from 'The investigators are extremely well qualified to achieve the proposed aims' (1) through 'The investigators do not appear to have adequate qualifications to achieve the proposed aims' (9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure biosketches, personal statements, and mentor involvement demonstrate qualifications and roles to meet higher descriptor levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation scoring descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptors judge novelty and degree of change: from 'Groundbreaking concepts, approaches, methodologies, or interventions that are novel for any research field' (1) down to 'No change of the current concepts, approaches, methodologies, or interventions' (9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly frame how concepts/methods are novel and the breadth of novelty (cross-field vs field-specific vs refinements) to align with higher descriptor levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach scoring descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptors evaluate likelihood the approach will achieve proposed aims, from 'The approach has an extremely high likelihood of achieving the proposed aims' (1) to 'The approach is unlikely to achieve most of the proposed aims' (9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide rigorous, feasible study design, appropriate statistical analysis, preliminary data, and contingency plans to increase Approach descriptor rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment scoring descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptors assess institutional resources and environment, from providing 'outstanding resources... including uncommon or unique resources' (1) to 'The environment does not appear to provide resources needed to achieve the proposed aims' (9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document institutional support, unique resources, core facilities, and mentorship environment to strengthen this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: General scoring descriptor labels mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric scores map to verbal descriptors (1 Exceptional, 2 Outstanding, 3 Excellent, 4 Very Good, 5 Good, 6 Satisfactory, 7 Fair, 8 Marginal, 9 Poor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how numeric scores correspond to descriptive judgments and that reviewers will use these labels when summarizing strengths/weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop preparation and peer feedback expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Trainees should bring fully prepared texts of proposals (Abstract, Specific Aims, Significance, Innovation, Approach) stored on a laptop; texts will be projected for group discussion and critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for real-time modification based on facilitator/peer comments. Each grant will receive about an hour of discussion focusing on organization, style, and clarity; trainees are encouraged to edit in real time.
